Outpacing the 0.3% rise in the S&P 500 (as of this writing) during today's market session, Vicor (NASDAQ:VICR) stock is climbing on the company's report of surprisingly strong third-quarter 2026 financial results released this morning before the opening bell.

As of 2:58 p.m. ET, shares of the modular power components manufacturer are up 7.4%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Revenue rises 78.5% year-over-year to $197.1 million

Beating analysts' expectations of $187 million, Vicor reported Q3 2026 revenue of $197.1 million, a quarter-over-quarter increase of 37.5% and a 78.5% increase over the same period last year.

At the bottom of the income statement, Vicor also provided a surprise, reporting net income of $63.3 million, or $1.33 per diluted share, compared to $28.3 million, or $0.63 per diluted share, in Q3 2025. Analysts had anticipated Vicor posting diluted earnings per share of $1.24 for Q3 2026.

It wasn't merely the insight into the company's recent financial performance that investors celebrated, however. Vicor reported a backlog totaling $406 million as of the end of September 2026 -- a 166% increase from the $153 million it had at the end of September 2025.

Is it too late to load up on Vicor stock?

Because it licenses its power system technologies to hyper-scalers, Vicor has emerged as yet another artificial intelligence (AI) stock investment opportunity -- specifically one that provides data center exposure. And while the hype around AI investments has waned recently, Vicor stock is still up about 87% since the start of the year. And with the impressive performance, Vicor's stock has now soared to a rich valuation. Currently, shares are trading at 75.8 times operating cash flow, a premium to its five-year average cash flow multiple of 36.6. At this point, investors should wait for the stock to experience a pullback before they choose to pull the trigger on a Vicor investment.

title: Ed Yardeni spots a major shakeup in the S&P 500
detail:
Ed Yardeni spots a major shakeup in the S&P 500
Moz Farooque
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 11:18 AM MST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
TSLA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

You don't need to own shares of Nvidia (NVDA) or Tesla (TSLA) individually to have a sizable bet on Big Tech.

Anyone who owns an S&P 500 index fund already owns both, along with other stocks that comprise the Magnificent Seven. Collectively, those seven companies account for nearly 35% of the benchmark. 

Truth be told, for the better part of the past three years, that concentration was a good thing. Big Tech powered the market higher, driving record gains in retirement and brokerage accounts.

For perspective, Fidelity Investments reported that average 401(k) balances reached a record $155,800 in Q2 2026, up 13% year over year, backed by market gains and continued savings.

Also read: 40-year market veteran shares S&P 500 outlook for 2027

But something has changed in 2026.

Wall Street veteran Ed Yardeni, who has spent years favoring major technology stocks, says the S&P 500's other 493 companies are now outperforming the celebrated seven.

And he thinks the shift has a lot to do with who's paying for the AI boom, and who's positioned to profit from it.

Ed Yardeni says S&P 493 stocks are now outperforming the Magnificent Seven.
ANGELA WEISS / Getty Images
The Magnificent Seven are no longer running away from the S&P 493 

For years, especially since the AI boom took off following the release of OpenAI's ChatGPT, betting on America's biggest tech companies has been one of the easiest ways to outperform the broader stock market.

The Magnificent Seven, which includes Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Nvidia (NVDA), Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL), Meta Platforms (META), and Tesla (TSLA), were almost unstoppable.

In 2023, the group surged 76%, compared with just 11% for the other 493 companies in the S&P 500, according to J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

The dominance persisted in 2024, when the seven gained 48% versus 14% for the rest. In 2025, they won again, returning 23% compared with 13%.

That's a tremendous run, particularly given how much these stocks influence the retirement accounts and index funds owned by millions of Americans.

But 2026 is telling a different story.

In his October 19 market commentary, veteran Wall Street strategist Ed Yardeni reported that his "Impressive 493" had gained 14.1% year-to-date, outperforming the Magnificent Seven's 10.2%, based on his ETF comparison.

Yardeni foresees a shakeup coming.

In December 2025, after roughly 15 years of favoring major technology stocks, he recommended underweighting the Magnificent Seven, anticipating stronger competition and better opportunities elsewhere in the market, as reported by Reuters.

Interestingly, the shift isn't happening because Big Tech's profits have fallen off a cliff.

(Updates with index/price moves and company/geopolitical news from the first paragraph.)

US equity indexes rose amid strong quarterly corporate results, while a disappointing initial public offering by a South Korean firm failed to dampen the risk sentiment in the AI trade.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 1% to 52,503.5, the S&P 500 climbed 0.4% to 7,723.8, and the Nasdaq Composite edged up 0.2% to 26,486.4 after midday Tuesday.

Equifax (EFX) reported a jump in Q3 adjusted earnings and operating revenue. Its shares soared 11%, the top gainer on the S&P 500.

Hasbro (HAS) reported fiscal Q3 adjusted earnings above market forecasts. The toy and game maker raised its fiscal 2026 constant-currency sales growth outlook. Shares jumped 9.4%, the second-biggest outperformer on the S&P 500.

3M (MMM) raised its full-year earnings outlook as the industrial conglomerate's Q3 bottom line topped market estimates. Shares advanced 5.8%, among the leaders on the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq.

Eight of the top 10 stocks in a category with market capitalization exceeding $200 billion were from the healthcare sector, and the remaining two from technology, including Oracle (ORCL), according to data compiled by Finviz. AstraZeneca (AZN) said it will combine its expertise with Oracle's cloud, data, and AI-enabled skills to advance clinical trial optimization.

The iShares PHLX Semiconductor Exchange Traded Fund (SOXX), with about $48.43 billion in assets under management, edged up 0.5%, the second consecutive day of gains in 11, reflecting investors continuing to dip toes back in following last week's sharp sell-off. The AI trade overcame South Korea's AI infrastructure and cloud company, Elice's (0158S0.KQ) 32% share-price drop at its KOSDAQ Market debut.

Further, Salesforce (CRM) agreed to acquire customer engagement platform Braze (BRZE) in a $5.66 billion deal to strengthen its business-to-consumer marketing solutions.

In geopolitical news, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy was due to meet US special envoy Steve Witkoff on Tuesday to rescue bilateral relations that have sunk to new lows after Kyiv complained about Washington withholding vital defenses, Reuters reported.

The UK will provide additional defensive military support to Saudi Arabia following escalating attacks in the region by Iran-aligned militant group Houthis. It will fly defensive counter-air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets, according to a UK government statement. These aircraft will operate defensively rather than conducting offensive strikes.

The front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil contract slid 0.7% to $97.85 per barrel, and global benchmark Brent declined 0.8% to $108.68 per barrel.

In economic news, housing starts fell 5.2% sequentially to a 1.22 million units rate in September, its lowest level since May, the Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development said. Based on an unrevised August reading, the consensus was 1.31 million in a Bloomberg-compiled survey.

Building permits, a forward-looking indicator of homebuilding, edged down 0.2% to 1.4 million units in September, compared with a 1.3% decline estimated by the Street. The print marked the second consecutive decline in permits.

US Treasury yields traded mixed after midday, with the two-year up 3.4 basis points to 4.80%. The 10-year yield was little changed at 5.13%, while the 30-year rate fell 3.3 basis points to 5.44%.

Gold futures declined 0.6% to $4,137.7, while silver futures rose 1.1% to $57.92.

Heading into the homestretch of 2026, there are some questions about the stock markets. This year, we've seen an energy shock, a shift toward a more hawkish monetary policy outlook, and the highest interest rates since 2002 – but the S&P 500 is up some 12% year-to-date.

Corporate earnings are the main driver of those market gains. The Q3 earnings have started coming in, and the consensus is for another quarter of double-digit gain – as much as 29%, by some estimates. Hitting this mark will give us eight quarters in a row of double-digit earnings gains.

And better yet, the gains have been growing broader through the year. The 'Magnificent 7' tech giants led the way last year, but this year their stocks have lagged parts of the broader market, while earnings growth has begun spreading beyond the group. Five S&P 500 sectors are now expected to deliver double-digit year-over-year earnings growth in Q3.

Writing about the general markets and the Q3 earnings, JPMorgan global investment strategist Kriti Gupta says: "Earnings expectations have been revised materially higher, as companies continue to exceed forecasts by significantly wider-than-expected margins. Early earnings results are reinforcing that narrative, with the vast majority already beating estimates… Can the blockbuster gains continue? If the early signals are any indication, the story that has defined the stock market in 2026 will likely remain intact: Corporate America continues to deliver earnings growth that is stronger, broader and more resilient than expected."

With that in mind, the JPMorgan stock analysts are picking out shares that are primed to win in the final stretch. We've opened the TipRanks database to look under the hood at two of the bank's 'top picks' for the rest of 2026; here they are, presented with the latest data and the JPM comments.

Argan (AGX)

Argan, the first company we'll look at, is a utility/industrial company working to build the next generation of 'traditional' power plants and teledata services. The company operates through a group of four subsidiaries, two of which – Gemma Power Systems and Atlantic Projects – specialize in providing innovative solutions for the power industry. Gemma is known as a leading building of combined cycle gas turbines, a highly efficient power generation system that makes use of the high-temperature exhaust produced in gas turbine generators to run a secondary steam turbine. Combined cycle gas turbines, or CCGTs, can generate as much as 50% more power per unit of fuel burned, while also generating a lower exhaust emission profile.

(Updates with latest market prices and developments.)

US benchmark equity indexes rose intraday supported by solid earnings, while traders looked ahead to quarterly results from SpaceX (SPCX) and Netflix (NFLX).

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.9% at 52,437.8 after midday Tuesday, while the S&P 500 advanced 0.3% to 7,714.1. The Nasdaq Composite edged up 0.1% to 26,458.5. Among sectors, healthcare paced the gainers, while communication services led the laggards.

Shares of 3M jumped 6% intraday, the best performer on the Dow and among the top gainers on the S&P 500. The industrial conglomerate raised its full-year earnings outlook as its third-quarter bottom line topped market estimates.

Hasbro (HAS) upgraded its full-year sales outlook after third-quarter results topped Wall Street's expectations, boosted by rising demand for its gaming portfolio. The toymaker's shares climbed 8.1%, the second-biggest gain on the S&P 500.

Northrop Grumman (NOC) rose 5.1%, also among the big winners on S&P 500, after the defense contractor upgraded its full-year profit outlook.

General Motors (GM) slumped 8.2%, the worst performer on the S&P 500. The Detroit automaker's updated 2026 profit guidance fell short of Wall Street's projections at the midpoint, overshadowing a third-quarter beat.

Among healthcare stocks, Moderna (MRNA) was up 5.8% intraday, among the notable gains on the S&P 500. UnitedHealth (UNH), Merck (MRK), Amgen (AMGN) and Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) also logged increases.

Rocket and satellite company SpaceX and streaming giant Netflix are scheduled to release their latest results after the market close Tuesday.

In a Monday client note, RBC Capital Markets said it expected SpaceX to continue sharing "ambitious" business updates with its financial results amid increasing investor interest around a potential merger with Tesla (TSLA).

Last week, Wedbush Securities said streaming giant Netflix is making significant changes to address slowing viewer engagement and revive growth, though the benefits may take time to materialize.

Treasury yields were mixed intraday, with the two-year rate gaining 3.4 basis points to 4.8% while the 10-year was little changed at 5.13%.

In economic news, US housing starts dropped to a four-month low in September amid declines in both single and multi-family units, while permits continued to trend downwards.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil edged up 0.3% to $103.98 a barrel intraday, while Brent dropped 0.6% to $108.90.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said Monday they launched several strikes at Saudi Arabia, targeting the Kingdom's energy, airport and military infrastructure, Reuters reported. Saudi authorities didn't immediately confirm the Houthi claims, the report showed.

Spot gold lost 0.3% to $4,127.46 per troy ounce, while silver gained 1.2% to $57.94 per ounce.
